outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the conjecture has been extended by a December 2025 preprint (Cranston) to all chromatic numbers r ≤ 24, and by a September 2026 preprint (Cao and Mehat) to r ≤ 29; a single-author preprint by Ankan Sadhu (v2, 13 September 2026) claims it for every r, but no refereed publication or qualified human check of that general claim was found, and the one automated review of its earlier version flagged an unverified step. The Fox–Pach–Suk results (SoCG 2025, arXiv October 2025) prove it only for graphs with at most about 1.4k to 1.64k vertices.
problem_asks: Part 1 (one universal claim): for every finite simple graph G, cr(G) ≥ cr(K_r), where r = χ(G) is the chromatic number of G and K_r is the complete graph on r vertices. Unpacked: (a) quantifies over all graphs G; (b) quantifies over every chromatic number r, so the claim is for all r ≥ 1 (r ≤ 4 trivial, r = 5 equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem); (c) the comparison object is the complete graph on the same number of vertices as the chromatic number; (d) the relation is a lower bound on cr(G) by cr(K_{χ(G)}), with no equality or strictness asked. The statement does not ask for the value of cr(K_r) (Guy's conjecture is related but not part of this bullet). Within this single inequality there is no further sub-question; every instance (fixed r, all graphs with χ = r) is part of the one claim.

events.what_happened: Oporowski and Zhao, 'Coloring graphs with crossings' (arXiv math/0501427, one version posted 25 January 2005; published in Discrete Mathematics 309(9), 2009 per the Wikipedia reference list). The arXiv abstract (opened) concerns extending the Five Colour Theorem to graphs with few crossings and does not mention Albertson's conjecture or chromatic number 6. Albertson, Cranston and Fox (2009) and Wikipedia attribute to Oporowski and Zhao the case r = 6 of Albertson's conjecture. I did not read the full arXiv text or the 2009 journal version, so I cannot say whether the r = 6 argument is in the 2005 posting.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (25 January 2005). Journal version Discrete Mathematics 309(9), 2009, per the Wikipedia reference list (not opened).
events.delivers: Attributed secondhand to this work: the case r = 6 (every graph with chromatic number 6 has crossing number at least cr(K_6)). Not stated in the arXiv abstract.
events.remains: Every r other than 6 for r ≥ 7 (the r ≤ 5 cases are trivial or equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem).

checked_by.who: Discrete Mathematics (journal of record), per the Wikipedia reference list
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2009). I did not verify the publication or read the r = 6 argument.

events.doubts: The r = 6 attribution rests on secondary citations (the 2009 Albertson–Cranston–Fox abstract and Wikipedia). The arXiv abstract does not state it, so the first public written date of the r = 6 argument is uncertain; I have used the arXiv posting date at year precision.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for r = 6.

events.what_happened: Albertson, Cranston and Fox, 'Crossings, colorings, and cliques', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 16 (2009), #R45. The arXiv version (arXiv:1006.3783, one version, submitted 18 June 2010, opened) states that the conjecture is proved for 7 ≤ r ≤ 12, that the case r = 5 is equivalent to the Four Colour Theorem, and that r = 6 was verified earlier by Oporowski and Zhao. Method per the abstract: lower bounds on the number of edges in critical graphs (Dirac, Gallai, Kostochka and Stiebitz) combined with crossing-number bounds in terms of edges and vertices. Wikipedia also says the paper gives a short proof of Schaefer's weaker bound χ = O(cr^(1/4)) (not read).
events.revisions: arXiv:1006.3783 v1 only, submitted 18 June 2010, after the journal volume date. The earlier date is the journal's.
events.delivers: For each r from 7 to 12, every graph with chromatic number r has crossing number at least cr(K_r). With r ≤ 6 (r = 6 secondhand), the covered range is all r ≤ 12.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 16 (2009), article R45. Listing seen in search results, article page not opened.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for 7 ≤ r ≤ 12.

events.what_happened: Barát and Tóth, 'Towards the Albertson conjecture', arXiv:0909.0413 (one version, submitted 2 September 2009; opened). The abstract states that the statement is proved for r ≤ 16, extending the r ≤ 12 result of Albertson, Cranston and Fox. Published in the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 17(1) (2010), article R73 (listing seen in search results, article page not opened).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only. Journal version EJC 17(1) R73, 2010.
events.delivers: For r = 13 to 16, every graph with chromatic number r has crossing number at least cr(K_r). Together with earlier results, all r ≤ 16.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in volume 17(1) (2010), article R73. Search listing only.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for 13 ≤ r ≤ 16.

events.what_happened: Luiz and Richter, 'Remarks on a Conjecture of Barát and Tóth', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 21(1) (2014), article P1.57, published 17 March 2014 (opened). This concerns whether r-critical graphs on r + c vertices contain a subdivision of K_r. Albertson's conjecture appears only as a keyword. Wikipedia says the paper gives, for every c ≥ 6, a family of (c+1)-colour-critical graphs with no subdivision of K_{c+1} but crossing number at least that of K_{c+1}; I did not confirm this in the paper.
events.revisions: Journal publication date. arXiv posting not checked.
events.delivers: Not a result on Albertson's conjecture. It concerns subdivisions of K_r in r-critical graphs (Hajós-type), a neighbouring question. Per Wikipedia (unverified here), it also gives crossing-number examples consistent with the conjecture.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (journal of record)

events.doubts: Neighbouring result, not an event on the problem as stated. Included so a later pass can see it; it bears on Albertson's conjecture only through the Barát–Tóth motivation.
events.direction: Does not address the inequality cr(G) ≥ cr(K_r) directly. It concerns a different (subdivision) statement.

events.what_happened: Ackerman, 'On topological graphs with at most four crossings per edge', arXiv:1509.01932 (v1 submitted 7 September 2015; v2 revised 24 March 2019; opened). The v1 abstract states: 'Our results imply that Albertson conjecture holds for r ≤ 18.' The main result is that a graph drawn with at most four crossings per edge has at most 6n − 12 edges, which gives cr(G) ≥ c m³/n² with c > 1/29. Wikipedia gives the journal version as Computational Geometry 85 (2019), 101574.
events.revisions: v1 7 September 2015 (the r ≤ 18 claim is in the v1 abstract); v2 24 March 2019; journal Computational Geometry 85 (2019) 101574 per Wikipedia.
events.delivers: For r ≤ 18 (new for r = 17 and 18), every graph with chromatic number r has crossing number at least cr(K_r). Achieved as a corollary of an edge bound for thin drawings, not by a direct argument on critical graphs.

checked_by.who: Computational Geometry (journal of record), per the Wikipedia reference list
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2019. Not opened.

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for r ≤ 18.

events.what_happened: Fox, Pach and Suk, 'Immersions and Albertson's Conjecture', 41st International Symposium on Computational Geometry (SoCG 2025), LIPIcs vol. 332, article 50, published 20 June 2025 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.SoCG.2025.50; abstract page opened). The abstract says the authors 'make some progress on Albertson's conjecture on crossing numbers of graphs', and that the conjecture 'is true for all graphs of chromatic number k' under the added conditions that the graph has at most 1.4(k − 1) vertices and k is sufficiently large. The same paper proves a weak-immersion version of the 1989 Lescure–Meyniel conjecture for those graphs. The full PDF was not read.
events.revisions: The arXiv version arXiv:2510.05893 (posted 7 October 2025) is a separate event below and carries a stronger vertex bound (1.64 − ε).
events.delivers: Restricted to graphs with at most 1.4(k − 1) vertices, for k sufficiently large (k not made explicit). For each such k, every graph with chromatic number k and at most 1.4(k − 1) vertices has cr(G) ≥ cr(K_k). All other graphs are untouched.
events.remains: Every graph with more than about 1.4(k − 1) vertices, for every chromatic number k; all k below the unspecified threshold.

checked_by.who: SoCG 2025 programme committee (refereed conference, LIPIcs proceedings)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed for a refereed computational geometry conference
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper into the proceedings. Refereeing details not read.

events.doubts: The abstract is the only text I read for this version. Whether the SoCG PDF contains the optimisation acknowledgement quoted in the later arXiv event is unknown.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for graphs with at most 1.4(k − 1) vertices and k large.

events.what_happened: Fox, Pach and Suk, 'Immersions and Albertson's conjecture', arXiv:2510.05893 (one version, submitted 7 October 2025; HTML rendering opened). Theorem 1.4 states: for every graph G with n ≤ (1.64 − ε)k vertices and chromatic number k, cr(G) ≥ cr(K_k), for every ε > 0 and sufficiently large k = k(ε). Theorem 1.2(i) gives the weak-immersion statement for n < 1.4k − 0.6, and Theorem 1.2(ii) gives the weak-immersion statement for n < (1.64 − ε)k. The acknowledgements say: 'Parts of the solution to this optimization problem in Section 3 were found with help from David Fox and Chat GPT-5.' The optimisation is Claim 3.7 (the maximum of an expression in α, γ, δ = 9/8 is 9/16), and by my reading of the formulas the 1.64 constant depends on that 9/16. The HTML page titles Section 3 'Proof of Lemma 2.3'.
events.revisions: v1 only (7 October 2025). Same title as the SoCG paper; the bound differs from the SoCG version (1.4(k − 1) there).
events.delivers: For sufficiently large k, every graph with chromatic number k and at most (1.64 − ε)k vertices has cr(G) ≥ cr(K_k). Restricted by vertex count and by an unspecified large-k threshold.
events.remains: Every graph with more than about 1.64k vertices; all k below the threshold; the general conjecture.
events.doubts: Only one version, posted after the SoCG paper, with a stronger bound. The 1.64 constant depends on Claim 3.7 whose maximum was found 'with help from' an AI system and a human; the paper states no separate verification beyond the case analysis in that proof. No public engagement with this version found.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for graphs with at most (1.64 − ε)k vertices and k large.
people: David Fox (credited in acknowledgements for help on the optimisation)

systems.name: Chat GPT-5
systems.what_it_did: Credited with help in finding parts of the solution to the optimisation problem in Claim 3.7 (maximum 9/16), which the paper's 1.64 vertex bound depends on. The authors do not say what share of the solution it produced.
systems.basis_quote: Parts of the solution to this optimization problem in Section 3 were found with help from David Fox and Chat GPT-5.

events.what_happened: Cranston, 'Progress on Albertson's Conjecture', arXiv:2512.08020 (sole author, one version, submitted 8 December 2025; abstract and HTML rendering opened). The abstract states 'Here we verify it for r ≤ 24; we also greatly restrict the possibilities for counterexamples when r ∈ {25, 26}.' Theorem 2 (per the HTML) says that for r ≤ 26 a counterexample must be an r-critical graph of order (25, 48), (26, 50) or (26, 51). Structural results for a minimal counterexample: order 2.82r or more excluded; 1.228r ≤ |G| ≤ 1.768r excluded; for r ≥ 125,000 the range 1.10r to 1.768r is excluded, and for r ≥ 825,000 the range 1.05r to 1.768r. The HTML says the table can be generated by a short Python program in Appendix B.
events.delivers: Verifies the conjecture for all r ≤ 24 (the r ≤ 24 verification is for all graphs with chromatic number r). For r = 25 and 26, reduces any counterexample to finitely many residual parameter pairs; the paper does not claim to settle r = 25 or 26. Also gives order restrictions on a minimal counterexample for all large r.
events.remains: Every r ≥ 25 for the full statement (r = 25 and 26 partly reduced to residual cases; all r ≥ 27 untouched).
events.doubts: The r ≤ 24 verification relies in part on a computer-generated table (Appendix B Python program); I found no independent check of that computation in print. Single author, no journal publication found. Later papers build on the reduction (see later_work_cites_it), but I found no public written check of the argument itself.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for r ≤ 24, and restricts any counterexample for r = 25, 26.

events.what_happened: Heejae Jung, 'A 15/31 Counterexample Family to the Albertson-Berman Conjecture', arXiv:2608.17350 (v1, submitted 18 August 2026; abstract opened). This concerns the Albertson–Berman conjecture (1979: every planar graph has an induced forest on at least half its vertices), not the crossing-number conjecture. The abstract says: 'We disprove the conjecture with an explicit 31-vertex plane triangulation T satisfying a(T) = 15.' Included because the names are the same and search summaries mixed the two.
events.delivers: A counterexample to the Albertson–Berman conjecture on induced forests in planar graphs. Nothing about cr(G) versus cr(K_r).
events.remains: The whole of the crossing-number conjecture.
events.directly_checkable: Per the arXiv comments: an ancillary Python verifier is included. Not run or read.
events.direction: Counterexample to a different conjecture (Albertson–Berman). It does not cut either way on the crossing-number statement.
events.object: An explicit 31-vertex plane triangulation T with maximum induced forest order a(T) = 15, claimed as a counterexample to the Albertson–Berman conjecture. Not the crossing-number problem.

events.what_happened: Cames van Batenburg, Goedgebeur and Jooken, 'Counterexamples to the Albertson-Berman conjecture: minimum order, connectivity and an improved ratio bound', arXiv:2608.23260 (v1, submitted 24 August 2026; abstract opened). This is about the Albertson–Berman conjecture, not the crossing-number conjecture. Claims: minimum order of a counterexample is 29; infinitely many 4-connected, 5-edge-connected counterexamples; planar families whose maximum induced forest has order at most 25/52 of the vertex count; counterexamples to a Chappell–Pelsmajer conjecture for every degree bound d ≥ 7. The abstract attributes the work to 'mathematical arguments and exhaustive computations'.
events.delivers: Results on the Albertson–Berman conjecture only. Nothing about the crossing-number conjecture.
events.remains: The whole of the crossing-number conjecture.
events.direction: Counterexamples to a different conjecture (Albertson–Berman). Does not cut either way on the crossing-number statement.
events.object: Planar graphs of order 29 whose largest induced forest has 14 vertices (two such graphs), and infinite families of 4-connected, 5-edge-connected planar counterexamples. For the Albertson–Berman conjecture only.

events.what_happened: Ankan Sadhu (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Government College of Engineering and Ceramic Technology, Kolkata), 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26', arXiv:2609.01682 v1, submitted 1 September 2026 (HTML v1 opened). The v1 abstract states: 'We prove it for r ∈ {25, 26}.' The HTML also states that the numerical assertions 'have been checked by machine in exact rational arithmetic.' Cao and Mehat (below) cite this version as having proved r ≤ 26.
events.revisions: v2 submitted 13 September 2026 (see sadhu-2026-v2-all-r): retitled 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture' and extended to all r. The arXiv abstract page still shows the v1 title.
events.delivers: Claims the conjecture for r = 25 and r = 26, on top of Cranston's r ≤ 24. Together that is r ≤ 26 under this version.
events.remains: Every r ≥ 27 (the all-r claim belongs to v2).

checked_by.who: Pith AI referee (Pith's T0 automated review; the model is named by the review as deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash)
checked_by.qualification: Automated; not a human reading. The review itself states 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.'
checked_by.what_they_did: Read v1 on 8 September 2026. Verdict: 'A careful, machine-checked extension of Albertson's conjecture through r=26.' Major objection: the r = 25, 26 dispatch depends on a crossing bound cr(H) ≥ 5|E(H)| − (203/9)(|V(H)|−2) (Lemma 2.1, citing Theorem 6(b) of reference [6]) without a density hypothesis; the reviewer could not verify it from the manuscript. Five minor objections (a 'Theorem 3.1' that should read 'Lemma 3.1', an unclear Table 1 column, rounding notation, an inequality in Appendix A given as 2480 > 2475 not in exact form, and a denominator in Lemma 2.2 eq. (1)).

events.directly_checkable: The HTML v1 says the numerical assertions were checked by machine in exact rational arithmetic. No archived artefact read for v1.
events.doubts: (a) The only review found is automated and flags a cited crossing bound with an unverified hypothesis that the r = 25, 26 dispatch needs. (b) No human expert engagement found. (c) Cao and Mehat cite it as having 'independently proved' r ≤ 26, so it has at least one reader, though that is a citation, not a check.
events.direction: Proves the conjecture for r = 25 and 26 (the lower bound); no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Sen Cao (Wuchang Shouyi College, Wuhan) and Sanjit Singh Mehat (independent researcher, United States), 'Albertson's Conjecture for Chromatic Numbers at Most 29: Critical graphs, essential immersions, Tutte barriers, and crossing-number sampling', arXiv:2609.04771 (one version, submitted 4 September 2026; abstract and HTML rendering opened). Theorem 1.1 is stated for every 1 ≤ r ≤ 29. Per the abstract (paraphrased in the fetch), the paper builds on Cranston's r ≤ 24 result and reduces r = 25, 26 to three residual cases, then 'eliminate[s] those residual cases and then prove[s] the cases r = 27, 28, 29'. Method per the abstract: a k-critical graph with a vertex of degree k − 1 contains an essential immersion of K_k, so a minimal counterexample has minimum degree at least k; for r = 27 structural and edge-count arguments; for r = 28 and 29, dense complements with Stehlík's colouring theorem, Tutte barriers and Hall-type arguments. The paper says Sadhu 'independently proved Albertson's conjecture for r ≤ 26' and that its own r = 25, 26, 27 work 'had already been completed and circulated prior to the appearance of Sadhu's preprint'. The AI statement, verbatim: 'Generative AI tools, including large language models, were used substantially during the development of this work'; 'AI-generated outputs were treated as provisional and were subject to human review'; 'The human authors take full responsibility for all mathematical statements, proofs, citations'. No model is named.
events.delivers: Every graph with chromatic number r, for each r from 1 to 29, has cr(G) ≥ cr(K_r) (the claim for r ≤ 24 is Cranston's, r = 25 and 26 are claimed here, and r = 27 to 29 are claimed here). Not for r ≥ 30.
events.directly_checkable: No computer artefact identified in the text I read (abstract page, HTML, and the 6.3 excerpt in a search summary). The HTML's reference list cites Sadhu's paper and Cranston's, not any software.
events.doubts: Preprint with no public human check found. Its r = 25, 26 claim overlaps Sadhu v1, and its priority statement ('already been completed and circulated') is the authors' own and not verifiable from the record. Parts of the proof for r = 28, 29 depend on a case analysis I did not read.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: proves the lower bound for 1 ≤ r ≤ 29 (r = 25, 26 claimed by this version as well as Sadhu's v1).

events.what_happened: Sadhu, 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture', arXiv:2609.01682 v2, submitted 13 September 2026 (HTML v2 opened). It claims the conjecture for every integer r, reducing a minimal counterexample to two order ranges. For large r: Gallai's decomposition, graph completion and a reserved weak-immersion routing argument. For the middle range: a bound on the number of edges, derived from repeated reductions on independent triples, combined with sampled crossing-number inequalities. The remaining finite and interval inequalities are checked by exact certificates; the text says 'Running python verify.py checks the certificates using exact integer and rational arithmetic; no solver or floating-point comparison is used.' The finite cases depend on certificate files (for example cert/near_residual.bin) said to be archived on GitHub and Zenodo. The v2 paper cites Cao and Mehat [6] and Cranston [7]. It also contains a generative-AI declaration (absent from v1): 'ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used for literature-search, language-editing, and verification assistance.' and 'The author reviewed the resulting manuscript and takes responsibility for its mathematical claims, computations, references, and conclusions.' (The second sentence is as the fetch rendered it.)
events.revisions: v1 1 September 2026 (r ≤ 26, title 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26'); v2 13 September 2026 (all r, title 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture'). The v2 scope is new material for r ≥ 27.
events.delivers: Claims the conjecture for every r, hence the full statement. Depends on Cranston's order reduction and on the certificate computations.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim holds. The claim has not been checked by anyone I could find.
events.directly_checkable: Certificate verifier verify.py (exact integer and rational arithmetic, per the v2 introduction) and certificate files said to be on GitHub and Zenodo. The GitHub repository URL found in search (github.com/Alphoenixx/albertson-conjecture-verification) returned HTTP 404 when fetched. Zenodo was not checked. Not run.
events.doubts: (a) Scope grew from r ≤ 26 (v1) to all r (v2), and the title changed; the all-r material is new in v2 and I found no public engagement with it. (b) The only review of v1 (Pith's automated AI referee) flagged an imported crossing-lemma hypothesis for r = 25, 26 that it could not verify; I found no reply or resolution in v2. (c) Finite and interval inequalities rest on certificate files I could not inspect. (d) Wikipedia (last edit reported by the fetch as 9 October 2026) and ProofAtlas (status checked 2 August 2026) still describe the conjecture as open, and neither mentions Sadhu's preprints. (e) The v2 declaration says ChatGPT was used for 'verification assistance', without saying what it verified.
events.direction: Proves the conjecture for every r (the lower bound); no counterexample claimed.

disputes.summary: r = 25 and 26: Sadhu's v1 (1 September 2026) claims both. Cao and Mehat (4 September 2026) say their own r = 25, 26 and 27 work 'had already been completed and circulated prior to the appearance of Sadhu's preprint'. I found no record of that earlier circulation; the arXiv timestamps favour Sadhu's posting. Both claims are unrefereed.

Sadhu's arXiv abstract page still shows the v1 title, 'Albertson's Conjecture Holds for r at Most 26', while the v2 text is titled 'A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture' and claims every r. The v1 HTML abstract says 'We prove it for r ∈ {25, 26}'. Cao and Mehat's bibliography cites the r ≤ 26 title. Each version's scope should be read separately.

The Albertson conjecture (crossing number vs chromatic number) is often confused with the Albertson–Berman conjecture (induced forests in planar graphs). Two 2026 papers (Jung; Cames van Batenburg, Goedgebeur and Jooken) concern the latter and are not events on this problem. A search summary also attributed the Albertson–Berman counterexample to GPT-5.6 Sol; I could not find that attribution on either abstract page.

summary: Nothing has settled the full conjecture in a refereed or expert-checked way since 26 January 2024. The position as I find it: (1) Cranston's single-author preprint (8 December 2025, arXiv:2512.08020) verifies r ≤ 24 and restricts counterexamples for r = 25, 26; it is not in a journal and I found no written check of its argument. (2) Fox, Pach and Suk (SoCG 2025, refereed; arXiv:2510.05893, October 2025) prove the conjecture for graphs with at most about 1.4(k − 1) vertices (SoCG) and at most (1.64 − ε)k vertices (arXiv), for k large and not made explicit. (3) Cao and Mehat (4 September 2026, arXiv:2609.04771) claim 1 ≤ r ≤ 29. (4) Sadhu (arXiv:2609.01682) posted v1 on 1 September 2026 claiming r ∈ {25, 26}, and v2 on 13 September 2026 claiming every r. The only review of v1 is by Pith's automated AI referee (named as deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash), which calls it 'careful, machine-checked' through r = 26 but raises a major objection that an imported crossing bound with a density hypothesis is unverified for r = 25, 26 (Lemma 2.1, citing Theorem 6(b) of reference [6]); the review states 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.' I found no human engagement with v2, which is about four weeks old. Two readings of (4) matter: it is a full proof two independent groups have each partly reproduced for r ≤ 26 and that Cao and Mehat cite as independent, or it is an unreviewed preprint whose all-r extension is new in v2 and has not been checked. Refereed results before the window: r = 6 (Oporowski–Zhao, arXiv 2005, journal 2009, attributed secondhand), r ≤ 12 (Albertson–Cranston–Fox, 2009), r ≤ 16 (Barát–Tóth, arXiv 2 September 2009, EJC 2010), r ≤ 18 (Ackerman, arXiv 7 September 2015, Computational Geometry 2019). Wikipedia (fetch reports last edit 9 October 2026) still says the relationship is unproven and cites none of the 2025–26 preprints. AI involvement: three in-window items name or describe AI. (i) Fox–Pach–Suk's arXiv acknowledgements credit 'Chat GPT-5' with helping find parts of the solution to the optimisation in Claim 3.7 (maximum 9/16), which I read as feeding the 1.64 bound; this is the only named system credited with mathematics in the record. The SoCG version's acknowledgements were not read. (ii) Cao and Mehat declare that 'Generative AI tools, including large language models, were used substantially during the development of this work' and name no system, so nothing is recorded in ai.systems; what the tools did is not specified beyond the declaration. (iii) Sadhu v2 declares 'ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used for literature-search, language-editing, and verification assistance', which on its face is not load-bearing mathematics, though 'verification assistance' is undefined. Sadhu v1 has no declaration. Cranston shows no AI mention. No AI-generated counterexample or AI-credited full proof was found for this conjecture. Close calls: whether Sadhu's v2 counts as a settlement of the all-r statement (scope grew from v1 and nobody has checked v2); whether the ChatGPT 'verification assistance' in v2 was load-bearing; and whether the 'Chat GPT-5' contribution to the 9/16 optimisation is load-bearing for the 1.64 bound or only for the expression of its proof. Related but separate: two 2026 papers on the Albertson–Berman conjecture (planar induced forests) report counterexamples; they are a different problem and are recorded as events only to keep the name collision visible. A search summary tying GPT-5.6 Sol to one of them could not be confirmed. The AIM workshop 'Albertson conjecture and related problems' (14–18 October 2024, organised by Pach, Suk and Tóth) is community activity and not a mathematical result; its report PDF was not readable. ProofAtlas, an AI-first research site (status checked 2 August 2026), lists the conjecture as open; it names no model and states no operator.
competing_reading: Sadhu v2 is a complete proof: it has exact-arithmetic certificates for the finite part, a human author who takes responsibility, a stated structure (Gallai decomposition, weak immersions, edge bounds), and an independent group (Cao and Mehat) that cites the r ≤ 26 part as correct. On that reading the problem is settled for all r as of 13 September 2026, and the AI declaration is ancillary. The opposing reading: the all-r material is new in v2, the only review of v1 flagged an unverified imported lemma for the r = 25, 26 part that v2 presumably also relies on, nobody has checked v2, and the certificate files were not inspected here (the GitHub artefact returned 404). On this reading the all-r claim is unestablished, and the established frontier is Cranston's r ≤ 24 plus Cao–Mehat's r ≤ 29, which is also unrefereed. A third reading affects only the AI question: Fox–Pach–Suk's credit to 'Chat GPT-5' describes help with a single optimisation, which a reader could treat as a computation tool rather than contributing the idea; the authors say 'parts of the solution' were 'found with help from', not that the system produced the claim.
what_would_settle_it: For the all-r status: a refereed publication of the all-r argument, or a named expert's written check of v2 (in particular the middle-range edge bound and the weak-immersion routing for large r), and a reply to the Lemma 2.1 hypothesis objection. For the r ≤ 29 status: the same for Cao and Mehat, plus clarity on the Sadhu priority claim. For the AI question: the SoCG 2025 acknowledgements (whether they repeat the Chat GPT-5 credit); what 'verification assistance' by ChatGPT in Sadhu v2 covered; and which generative AI tools Cao and Mehat used and for what. A working copy of the certificate files (GitHub or Zenodo) that runs and reproduces the finite inequalities would also bear on the all-r claim.
